idiom_name: Proc/lambda predicates with Enumerable#select, grep and case/when via #call and #===
implementation_notes: In Ruby a rule is a Proc or lambda - `overdue = ->(invoice) { invoice.days_past_due >= 30 }` - composition is a lambda calling the parts (`->(i) { overdue.(i) && !in_collection.(i) }`) or a tiny combinator, and Enumerable#select/find_all/any?/all? consume it. Because Proc#call is aliased by Proc#===, a rule also works as a case/when target and therefore with Enumerable#grep, which is Ruby's distinctive twist on the pattern; parameterized rules are factories returning lambdas. A rule object with a domain name (a class responding to #call or #is_satisfied_by) remains right for rules that must be logged, serialized or exposed as part of an API, and the database-side composition idiom is an ActiveRecord scope composed with Relation#merge - at the cost of coupling the rule to the ORM.
pitfalls: Proc and lambda semantics differ: a non-lambda proc's return/break exits the enclosing method (LocalJumpError when called later) and it ignores arity, so rules should be written as lambdas (->) rather than procs or bare blocks.
Blocks and procs capture self and the surrounding locals; a rule created in a loop shares the loop variable, and a rule closing over mutated state changes behaviour between calls.
Object#=== defaults to #==, so a custom rule class must define #=== (or expose #call and be wrapped in a Proc) before it works in case/when and grep.
In Rails, filtering a loaded relation in Ruby (select on the records) evaluates every row in memory; express the rule in the relation and compose with merge when the data set is large.
